New FEMA administrator says he wants to restore 'common sense' to agency

The uncertainty around the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) started when President Donald Trump in January 2025 said, “I think we’re going to recommend FEMA go away, and we pay directly to the state.”

That kicked off questions about whether the country’s disaster response agency would be abolished.

But four months later in May 2024, FEMA’s acting Administrator, Cameron Hamilton, was asked about the agency’s future and said, “I do not believe it is in the best interests of the American people to eliminate the Federal Emergency Management Agency.”

A day later, Hamilton was out of a job.

“Being asked to ultimately step aside and serve in another capacity was something at the discretion of my senior leadership,” Hamilton told Spectrum News in an October interview.

This past May, President Trump brought Hamilton back, nominating him to lead FEMA. In August, he was confirmed by the Senate, becoming the agency’s first permanent leader in a year and a half.

Spectrum News spoke exclusively with Hamilton in his first sit-down interview.

FEMA is under the Department of Homeland Security, which is no longer led by Kristi Noem, who led the agency when Hamilton was removed last year.

“Service is service no matter who you work for. I’ve worked for people that I admire and people I didn’t,” Hamilton said. “I’d say it’s an honor to serve no matter what.”

Hamilton is a former U.S. Navy SEAL and combat medic. He stated he aims to speed up assistance for disaster victims by streamlining bureaucracy, while also making sure FEMA’s role is to assist states post-disaster, not to lead.

“It’s our job to right size and pull it back to the proper context to ensure we provide them assistance but not supplant them in those authorities,” Hamilton said.

During fiscal year 2025, the agency shed 4,300 people from its workforce of around 25,000 people, according to the Government Accountability Office.

When asked if FEMA had enough staff for the current hurricane season, Hamilton said, “This agency is staffed far larger, frankly, than it ever has been with the exception of maybe the latter years of the Biden administration.”

Numbers compiled by USA Facts show FEMA’s workforce was around 14,000 in 2016 and climbed to over 25,000 in 2025. It now sits around 20,000.

The number of billion-dollar storms, however, has climbed, with nearly 50% happening from 2017 through the end of 2024.

Earlier this year, President Trump’s FEMA Review Council didn’t recommend eliminating FEMA but called for putting state and local governments on the hook for more money.

When asked about the uncertainty states and local governments have faced about FEMA’s future the past year-and-a-half, and whether they will have the money to respond to a disaster, Hamilton said, “What I would tell states is that if there is concern over whether they are able to have the financial resources… we would like to see them invest early…we’re here to be partners, we’re here to be as strong and capable as possible to deal with the high consequence events that every state will face.”

Hamilton told Spectrum News that President Trump has read the FEMA Review Council’s final report.

Asked whether the president will enact or recommend any of the changes in the report, a White House spokesperson told Spectrum News, “The President remains committed to getting resources to communities in need while also working with states to ensure they invest in their own resilience before disaster strikes, making response less urgent and recovery less prolonged.”

One of Hamilton’s first stops since taking over was western North Carolina to tour damage from Helene, which hit the state two years ago.

The Trump administration faced bipartisan criticism last year for not getting federal assistance money to the state fast enough.

In recent months, it has been agreed that the money flow has accelerated.

“We’ve moved a significant amount of resources. We still have a long way to go. But you’re right in calling out that there was a backlog. I think we’ve done a pretty good job of clearing a lot of that backlog recently,” Hamilton said.

Hamilton hopes to put an agency built for disaster on solid footing.

“Get back to good common sense, good sound business practices to ensure that the state and local counterparts can be empowered to make decisions,” Hamilton said. “Operationally focused, radically transparent, clear and predictable in execution and most importantly keeping the American people first.”
